title: Mathematics Foundations
desc: The mathematical toolkit behind everything in the academy. Work through these before or alongside the main sections — not a blocker, but a reference. Each unit tells you exactly which academy sections depend on it.

chapters.title: Core Mathematical Toolkit
chapters.sub: Linear algebra · Probability · Calculus · Differential equations

units.title: Linear Algebra
units.meta: Vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, SVD — the language of everything

watch.title: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra — Gilbert Strang (36 lectures, MIT OCW)
watch.focus: Priority lectures: 1 (geometry of linear equations), 6 (column space and null space), 14 (orthogonality), 21 (eigenvalues and eigenvectors), 29 (singular value decomposition). These 5 lectures cover the specific concepts used throughout the academy. Full course if you want the complete foundation.

concept.title: Why linear algebra is the backbone of the academy
concept.body:
Where it appears in the academy:

CV Section: Images are matrices (H×W×C tensors). Convolution is matrix multiplication. PCA for dimensionality reduction uses eigendecomposition. Camera projection is a matrix operation: p = K[R|t]P.

ML Section: Neural network forward pass: y = Wx + b (matrix-vector multiplication). Backpropagation: chain rule of matrix derivatives. Batch training: entire dataset as a matrix.

TDL Section: Covariance matrices for uncertainty. SVD for low-rank approximations. Multivariate Gaussian distributions represented as (μ, Σ).

Robotics Section: Every transform is a matrix. T ∈ SE(2) is a 3×3 matrix. EKF covariance updates are matrix operations. Circle fitting uses SVD (the NU ME495 14-step algorithm).
concept.analogy: Linear algebra is the universal language that all the other sections speak. When CS231N says 'convolution', when Kalman filter says 'covariance update', when CS229 says 'gradient descent' — they are all doing linear algebra. Understanding the language makes every other concept immediately clearer.
concept.visual:
Key concepts and where they appear:

Matrix multiplication  → Forward pass, transforms, projection
Eigendecomposition     → PCA, covariance ellipses, stability
SVD                    → Circle fitting (NU ME495), low-rank approx
Dot product            → Attention mechanisms, cosine similarity
Gaussian elimination   → Solving linear systems in kinematics
Determinant            → Volume scaling, invertibility checks

Self-assessment: can you explain why
T_AC = T_AB · T_BC without memorizing it?

challenge.q: A neural network layer has weight matrix W ∈ R^(512×256) and input x ∈ R^256. What is the shape of Wx, and how many multiplications does computing it require?

opts.t: Shape: R^(512×256), this is a matrix not a vector operation
Shape: R^512, multiplications: 512 (one per output element)

challenge.hint: W is 512 rows × 256 columns. x is a 256-dimensional vector. Matrix-vector multiplication: each output element is a dot product of one row of W with x.
challenge.exp: W ∈ R^(512×256) multiplied by x ∈ R^256 gives output y ∈ R^512. Each of the 512 output elements requires 256 multiplications (dot product of one row with x) = 512×256 = 131,072 multiplications total. For a batch of 32 inputs: 32×131,072 = ~4M multiplications — just for one layer. This is why GPUs (which parallelize matrix ops) are essential for deep learning.

units.title: Probability and Statistics
units.meta: Bayes theorem, distributions, expectation — the language of uncertainty

watch.title: Harvard Statistics 110 — Probability, Joe Blitzstein (34 lectures)
watch.focus: Priority lectures: 1 (probability and counting), 2 (story proofs, Vandermonde), 4 (conditional probability, Bayes theorem), 8 (random variables and distributions), 23 (Beta distribution), 29 (law of large numbers and CLT), 30 (Multivariate Normal). The edX companion (edx.org/course/introduction-to-probability-0) has interactive problems.

concept.title: Why probability is the language of robotics and trustworthy AI
concept.body:
Every major concept in the academy uses probability. Not as background — as the core language.

TDL Section: Uncertainty quantification = probability over predictions. Calibration = does P(correct | confidence=0.9) = 0.9? KL divergence = distance between probability distributions. Bayesian inference = updating beliefs with evidence.

Robotics Section (NU ME495): Robot pose is a probability distribution N(μ, Σ), not a point. The Kalman filter maintains a Gaussian belief. EKF-SLAM tracks joint probability over robot pose AND landmark positions. Every sensor reading is a random variable with noise model.

ML Section (CS229): Maximum Likelihood Estimation derives loss functions from probability. Logistic regression outputs probabilities. Generalization bounds come from concentration inequalities.
concept.analogy: In classical programming, variables have exact values. In the academy's world, variables have probability distributions — the robot is 'probably here', the model is 'probably correct with 87% confidence', the sensor reading is 'true distance plus Gaussian noise'. Probability is how you reason rigorously when you are uncertain.
concept.visual:
Key concepts and where they appear:

Bayes theorem          → Kalman update step, classification
Gaussian N(μ, Σ)      → Sensor noise, robot pose belief, KF state
CLT                    → Why Gaussian assumption is justified
MLE                    → Deriving cross-entropy loss from probability
Conditional expectation → EKF-SLAM cross-covariance terms
Markov chains           → State estimation, MCMC sampling

Self-assessment: given z = x + ε where ε~N(0,σ²),
can you write p(z|x) without looking it up?

challenge.q: A sensor measures distance with noise: z = d_true + ε where ε~N(0, 0.04). Your prior belief about the true distance is d~N(2.0, 0.09). You measure z=2.3m. What is the Kalman gain K?

opts.t: K cannot be computed without the measurement matrix H

challenge.hint: Kalman gain: K = σ²_prior / (σ²_prior + σ²_measurement). Think of it as: how much should I trust the measurement vs my prior?
challenge.exp: K = P/(P+R) = 0.09/(0.09+0.04) = 0.692. This means: the updated estimate moves 69.2% of the way from the prior (2.0m) toward the measurement (2.3m). Updated estimate = 2.0 + 0.692×(2.3-2.0) = 2.208m. Updated variance = (1-K)×P = 0.308×0.09 = 0.028. The posterior is tighter than either the prior or measurement alone — this is the Kalman filter magic.

units.title: Multivariate Calculus
units.meta: Gradients, Jacobians, chain rule — the engine of optimization and EKF

watch.title: 3Blue1Brown Essence of Calculus + MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus
watch.focus: Start with 3Blue1Brown Essence of Calculus videos 1-4 (youtube.com/playlist?list=PLZHQObOWTQDMsr9K-rj53DwVRMYO3t5Yr) for geometric intuition — watch all 11 videos (each ~15 min). Then MIT 18.02 (ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02-multivariable-calculus-fall-2007/) Lectures 1-15 for multivariate extension: partial derivatives, gradients, Jacobians, chain rule for vector functions.

concept.title: Gradients and Jacobians — two concepts that run the whole academy
concept.body:
Gradient ∇f: a vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase of a scalar function. Gradient descent moves opposite to the gradient. Every parameter update in every neural network uses the gradient of the loss w.r.t. parameters.

Jacobian J = ∂f/∂x: a matrix of all partial derivatives of a vector function. If f: R^n → R^m, then J ∈ R^(m×n). The Jacobian appears in: backpropagation (chain rule), EKF linearization (F = ∂f/∂x evaluated at current estimate), robot kinematics (velocity Jacobian).

Chain rule for vector functions: if z = f(g(x)), then ∂z/∂x = ∂f/∂g · ∂g/∂x (Jacobian multiplication). This is backpropagation.
concept.analogy: The gradient tells you which direction is uphill on a landscape. The Jacobian tells you how a multi-dimensional transformation stretches and rotates space locally. Backpropagation is just the chain rule applied recursively through layers — the Jacobian of each layer composed with the next.
concept.visual:
Gradient (scalar function f: R^n → R):
∇f = [∂f/∂x₁, ∂f/∂x₂, ..., ∂f/∂xₙ]ᵀ

Jacobian (vector function f: R^n → R^m):
J = ∂f/∂x  ∈ R^(m×n)
J_ij = ∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ

Chain rule (backpropagation):
if z = f(g(x)):
∂z/∂x = (∂f/∂g) · (∂g/∂x)  ← Jacobian product

EKF: F = ∂f/∂x |_{x̂}  evaluated at current estimate
This linearizes f locally — that's all EKF does.

challenge.q: Neural network: z = W₂·σ(W₁·x). You want ∂L/∂W₁ where L is the scalar loss. Which calculus concept gives you this?

opts.t: Gradient descent — you move W₁ in the negative gradient direction
Jacobian of L with respect to x — backprop flows through x not W
Partial derivative ∂L/∂W₁ computed by perturbing W₁ by ε (numerical)

challenge.hint: L depends on W₁ through the chain: W₁ → W₁x → σ(W₁x) → W₂σ(W₁x) → L. Which calculus rule handles composed functions?
challenge.exp: The chain rule: ∂L/∂W₁ = (∂L/∂z) · (∂z/∂a) · (∂a/∂W₁x) · (∂W₁x/∂W₁) where a = σ(W₁x). Each factor is a Jacobian. Backpropagation is this chain rule applied automatically through computational graphs. Numerical perturbation (option D) works but is O(n) times slower than analytical backprop — impractical for millions of parameters.

units.title: Differential Equations
units.meta: ODEs, dynamics, state equations — the physics of robot motion

watch.title: MIT 18.03SC Differential Equations — Arthur Mattuck (OCW Scholar format)
watch.focus: Priority lectures: 1 (geometric view of ODEs), 2 (Euler's numerical method), 3 (solving first-order linear ODEs), 7 (complex exponentials), 9-10 (second-order ODEs with constant coefficients). Full OCW Scholar course at ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-03sc-differential-equations-fall-2011/ includes interactive Java demos, problem sets, and solutions. Focus on first and second order ODEs for the academy.

concept.title: Where differential equations appear in the academy
concept.body:
Robotics Section Ch2 (Dynamics): Robot arm equations of motion: τ = M(θ)θ̈ + C(θ,θ̇)θ̇ + G(θ). This is a system of second-order ODEs. Gravity compensation requires solving G(θ). Trajectory simulation requires numerically integrating this ODE (scipy.integrate.odeint).

Kalman Filter derivation: The continuous-time Kalman filter is described by the Riccati differential equation dP/dt = AP + PAᵀ + Q - PCᵀR⁻¹CP. The discrete-time KF (what you implement) is the numerical integration of this ODE.

Hardware Section Ch4 (PID control): The PID controller error signal e(t) satisfies a differential equation. Stability analysis uses the characteristic equation of the closed-loop ODE.
concept.analogy: A differential equation describes how something changes over time as a function of its current state. Robot dynamics say: 'given the current joint angles and velocities, here is how they will accelerate.' The ODE encodes the physics. Numerical integration (Euler, RK4) lets you simulate it forward in time.
concept.visual:
Types of DEs in the academy:

First-order ODE (state estimation):
dx/dt = Ax + Bu  ← linear time-invariant system

Second-order ODE (robot dynamics):
M(θ)θ̈ = τ - C(θ,θ̇)θ̇ - G(θ)

Numerical integration (Euler method):
x_{k+1} = x_k + dt · f(x_k, u_k)

RK4 (more accurate, what scipy uses):
k1 = f(x_k)
k2 = f(x_k + dt/2 · k1)
k3 = f(x_k + dt/2 · k2)
k4 = f(x_k + dt · k3)
x_{k+1} = x_k + dt/6·(k1+2k2+2k3+k4)

challenge.q: You have robot dynamics ẍ = -2ẋ - 5x + u. At t=0: x=1, ẋ=0, u=0. After one Euler step with dt=0.1s, what is x(0.1)?

opts.t: Cannot compute without knowing the full trajectory

challenge.hint: Euler: x_{k+1} = x_k + dt·ẋ_k. ẋ_{k+1} = ẋ_k + dt·ẍ_k. Compute ẍ(0) first.
challenge.exp: ẍ(0) = -2×0 - 5×1 + 0 = -5. Euler step: x(0.1) = 1.0 + 0.1×0 = 1.0. ẋ(0.1) = 0 + 0.1×(-5) = -0.5. So after one step x stays at 1.0 but velocity is now -0.5 m/s (the spring force is pulling it back). After the next step x will decrease. This is why Euler integration with small dt captures the physics — each step applies the ODE locally.

assignment.title: Mathematical Self-Assessment
assignment.desc: A self-directed check: can you connect the math to what you are about to build? This is not graded — it is a diagnostic. Work through each item and note where you need to go deeper.
deliverables: Linear Algebra: implement matrix multiplication from scratch (no numpy), verify on a 3×3 transform composition
Probability: derive the Kalman gain formula K = P/(P+R) from scratch — start from the definition of the optimal linear estimator
Calculus: compute the Jacobian of f(x,y) = [x²+y, sin(x)·y] analytically, verify numerically
DiffEq: implement Euler integration for a simple pendulum θ̈ = -(g/L)sinθ, plot the trajectory for 10 seconds
README: one paragraph per topic — where does this math appear in the section you are about to start?
assignment.hint: None of these are meant to be hard. They are meant to surface gaps before you hit them inside a more complex unit. 2-3 hours total.
